claim: Cell-cell communication via gap junctions regulates a wide range of physiological processes by enabling the direct intercellular electrical and chemical coupling.
source: Cell-cell communication via gap junctions regulates a wide range of physiological processes by enabling the direct intercellular electrical and chemical coupling.
evidence: This is a general statement about gap junction function that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The in vivo distribution and function of gap junctions remain poorly understood, partly due to the lack of non-invasive tools with both cell-type specificity and high spatiotemporal resolution.
source: However, the in vivo distribution and function of gap junctions remain poorly understood, partly due to the lack of non-invasive tools with both cell-type specificity and high spatiotemporal resolution.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current methodology and understanding, representing the authors' assessment of the field.

claim: PARIS is a fully genetically encoded tool for measuring cell-specific gap junctional coupling (GJC).
source: Here, we developed PARIS (pairing actuators and receivers to optically isolate gap junctions), a new fully genetically encoded tool for measuring the cell-specific gap junctional coupling (GJC).
evidence: This is the main claim about the tool developed in this study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: PARIS successfully enabled monitoring of GJC in several cultured cell lines under physiologically relevant conditions.
source: PARIS successfully enabled monitoring of GJC in several cultured cell lines under physiologically relevant conditions and in distinct genetically defined neurons in Drosophila brain, with ~10 s temporal resolution and sub-cellular spatial resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3 demonstrating PARIS function in HEK293T cells, HeLa cells, and cardiomyocytes.

claim: PARIS successfully enabled monitoring of GJC in distinct genetically defined neurons in Drosophila brain.
source: PARIS successfully enabled monitoring of GJC in several cultured cell lines under physiologically relevant conditions and in distinct genetically defined neurons in Drosophila brain, with ~10 s temporal resolution and sub-cellular spatial resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5 demonstrating PARIS function in Drosophila neurons.

claim: PARIS has ~10 s temporal resolution.
source: PARIS successfully enabled monitoring of GJC in several cultured cell lines under physiologically relevant conditions and in distinct genetically defined neurons in Drosophila brain, with ~10 s temporal resolution and sub-cellular spatial resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic measurements shown in Figure 1G indicating half-rise times of approximately 10 seconds.

claim: PARIS has sub-cellular spatial resolution.
source: PARIS successfully enabled monitoring of GJC in several cultured cell lines under physiologically relevant conditions and in distinct genetically defined neurons in Drosophila brain, with ~10 s temporal resolution and sub-cellular spatial resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5 showing PARIS can distinguish gap junctions at dendrite-dendrite contacts in the AL versus axon-axon contacts in the LH.

claim: PARIS is a robust, highly sensitive tool for mapping functional gap junctions and studying their regulation in both health and disease.
source: These results demonstrate that PARIS is a robust, highly sensitive tool for mapping functional gap junctions and study their regulation in both health and disease.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript, including sensitivity measurements and applications to different systems.

claim: Gap junctions are intercellular channels that are expressed in virtually all tissue types in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Gap junctions are intercellular channels that are expressed in virtually all tissue types in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junction distribution across species.

claim: Gap junctions allow direct transfer of small molecules such as ions, metabolites and second messengers between connected cells.
source: They allow direct transfer of small molecules such as ions, metabolites and second messengers between connected cells, thereby playing essential roles in various physiological processes, including embryo development, metabolic coordination of avascular organs, tissue homeostasis and synchronizing electrical activity in excitable tissues (Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Kumar and Gilula, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on gap junction function.

claim: Gap junctions play essential roles in embryo development, metabolic coordination of avascular organs, tissue homeostasis and synchronizing electrical activity in excitable tissues.
source: They allow direct transfer of small molecules such as ions, metabolites and second messengers between connected cells, thereby playing essential roles in various physiological processes, including embryo development, metabolic coordination of avascular organs, tissue homeostasis and synchronizing electrical activity in excitable tissues (Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Kumar and Gilula, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on gap junction function.

claim: Defects of gap junction function are linked with myocardial infarction, hearing loss and hypomyelinating disorder.
source: Defects of gap junction function are linked with a wide array of diseases, including myocardial infarction, hearing loss and hypomyelinating disorder (Jongsma and Wilders, 2000; Laird, 2010; Söhl et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on gap junction-related diseases.

claim: Current methods used to monitor GJC include paired electrophysiological recordings, dye microinjection, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and local activation of molecular fluorescent probes (LAMP).
source: Current methods used to monitor GJC include paired electrophysiological recordings (Bennett et al., 1963; Furshpan and Potter, 1959), dye microinjection (Stewart, 1978), fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (Wade et al., 1986), and local activation of molecular fluorescent probes (LAMP) (Dakin et al., 2005), all of which are either invasive and/or lack cell-type specificity, thus limiting their use in heterogeneous tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original papers describing these methods.

claim: Current methods for monitoring GJC are either invasive and/or lack cell-type specificity, thus limiting their use in heterogeneous tissues.
source: Current methods used to monitor GJC include paired electrophysiological recordings (Bennett et al., 1963; Furshpan and Potter, 1959), dye microinjection (Stewart, 1978), fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (Wade et al., 1986), and local activation of molecular fluorescent probes (LAMP) (Dakin et al., 2005), all of which are either invasive and/or lack cell-type specificity, thus limiting their use in heterogeneous tissues.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of existing methods based on their characteristics.

claim: Hybrid approaches have been developed in which genetically encoded hydrolytic enzymes or promiscuous transporters are used to introduce small molecule substrates or peptides tagged with a fluorescent label in specific cells.
source: Recently, hybrid approaches have been developed in which genetically encoded hydrolytic enzymes or promiscuous transporters are used to introduce small molecule substrates or peptides tagged with a fluorescent label in specific cells (Qiao and Sanes, 2015; Tian et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to papers describing these hybrid approaches.

claim: Hybrid approaches for GJC detection require exogenous substrate and generate background from endogenous enzymes or transporters, making them difficult to apply in vivo.
source: Although these methods might provide cell-type-specific investigation of GJC, the requirement of exogenous substrate and the background generated by endogenous enzymes or transporters still make them difficult to apply in vivo.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of hybrid approaches based on their characteristics.

claim: Dye diffusion is an irreversible process and thus these methods are difficult to be applied to examine the same gap junctions repeatedly in order to measure their dynamics, regulations and plasticity.
source: In addition, dye diffusion is an irreversible process and thus these methods are difficult to be applied to examine the same gap junctions repeatedly in order to measure their dynamics, regulations and plasticity (Dong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a logical inference about the limitations of irreversible methods.

claim: PARIS expresses an optically controlled actuator in one cell to generate an electrochemical gradient of specific molecules between two connected cells.
source: To overcome these limitations, we developed an all-optical approach named PARIS (pairing actuators and receivers to optically isolate gap junctions) in which we express an optically controlled actuator in one cell, to generate an electrochemical gradient of specific molecules between two connected cells, and a fluorescent receiver in the adjacent cell, to detect the movement of the molecules across the gap junctions.
evidence: This describes the design principle of PARIS as implemented by the authors.

claim: PARIS expresses a fluorescent receiver in the adjacent cell to detect the movement of molecules across the gap junctions.
source: To overcome these limitations, we developed an all-optical approach named PARIS (pairing actuators and receivers to optically isolate gap junctions) in which we express an optically controlled actuator in one cell, to generate an electrochemical gradient of specific molecules between two connected cells, and a fluorescent receiver in the adjacent cell, to detect the movement of the molecules across the gap junctions.
evidence: This describes the design principle of PARIS as implemented by the authors.

claim: GJC between the actuator cell and the receiver cell is detected by a fluorescence increase in the receiver following the optical activation of the actuator.
source: GJC between the actuator cell (i.e. expressing actuators) and the receiver cell (i.e. expressing receivers) is detected by a fluorescence increase in the receiver following the optical activation of the actuator (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the readout mechanism of PARIS, supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: A light-activated cGMP cyclase BeCylOp paired with a cGMP sensor FlincG3 could not generate detectable light-induced signal when co-expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: We found that, when co-expressed in HEK293T cells (i.e. in the cis configuration), neither a light-activated cGMP cyclase BeCylOp (Gao et al., 2015) paired with a cGMP sensor FlincG3 (Bhargava et al., 2013) nor the red shifted channelrhodopsin CsChrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014) paired with a sensitive Ca2+ indicator GCaMP6s (Chen et al., 2013) could generate detectable light-induced signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The red shifted channelrhodopsin CsChrimson paired with a sensitive Ca2+ indicator GCaMP6s could not generate detectable light-induced signal when co-expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: We found that, when co-expressed in HEK293T cells (i.e. in the cis configuration), neither a light-activated cGMP cyclase BeCylOp (Gao et al., 2015) paired with a cGMP sensor FlincG3 (Bhargava et al., 2013) nor the red shifted channelrhodopsin CsChrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014) paired with a sensitive Ca2+ indicator GCaMP6s (Chen et al., 2013) could generate detectable light-induced signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When co-expressed in HEK293T cells, a light-gated outward proton pump ArchT and a pH-sensitive green fluorescent protein pHluorin generate a robust increase in pHluorin fluorescence upon 4 s laser illumination at 561 nm.
source: Interestingly, when we co-expressed a light-gated outward proton pump ArchT (Han et al., 2011) and a pH-sensitive green fluorescent protein pHluorin (Miesenböck et al., 1998; Sankaranarayanan et al., 2000) in HEK293T cells, a 4 s laser illumination at 561 nm elicited a robust increase in pHluorin fluorescence, with the membrane-targeted pHluorin (pHluorinCAAX) producing a larger change in fluorescence than the cytosolic pHluorin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Membrane-targeted pHluorin (pHluorinCAAX) produces a larger change in fluorescence than cytosolic pHluorin when co-expressed with ArchT.
source: Interestingly, when we co-expressed a light-gated outward proton pump ArchT (Han et al., 2011) and a pH-sensitive green fluorescent protein pHluorin (Miesenböck et al., 1998; Sankaranarayanan et al., 2000) in HEK293T cells, a 4 s laser illumination at 561 nm elicited a robust increase in pHluorin fluorescence, with the membrane-targeted pHluorin (pHluorinCAAX) producing a larger change in fluorescence than the cytosolic pHluorin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: No light-induced change in fluorescence was observed in cells co-expressing pHluorinCAAX and the deficient proton-pump ArchTD95N.
source: No light-induced change in fluorescence was observed in cells that co-expressing pHluorinCAAX and the deficient proton-pump ArchTD95N (Kralj et al., 2011), or in cells that only express pHluorinCAAX (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B and serves as a negative control.

claim: No light-induced change in fluorescence was observed in cells that only express pHluorinCAAX.
source: No light-induced change in fluorescence was observed in cells that co-expressing pHluorinCAAX and the deficient proton-pump ArchTD95N (Kralj et al., 2011), or in cells that only express pHluorinCAAX (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B and serves as a negative control.

claim: The evoked response from ArchT/pHluorin is dependent on both the duration and the power of the activating light.
source: Furthermore, the evoked response is dependent on both the duration and the power of the activating light (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F demonstrating dose-response relationships.

claim: ArchT and pHluorin can function as a pair of proton actuator and proton sensor.
source: These results demonstrate that ArchT and pHluorin can function as a pair of proton actuator and proton sensor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing that ArchT activation leads to pHluorin fluorescence changes.

claim: HEK293T cells endogenously express both connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx45.
source: We next examined whether PARIS based on ArchT/pHluorin can be used to measure GJC between cultured HEK293T cells, which endogenously express both connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx45, therefore spontaneously form gap junctions between adjacent cells (Butterweck et al., 1994; Langlois et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on HEK293T cell connexin expression.

claim: HEK293T cells spontaneously form gap junctions between adjacent cells.
source: We next examined whether PARIS based on ArchT/pHluorin can be used to measure GJC between cultured HEK293T cells, which endogenously express both connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx45, therefore spontaneously form gap junctions between adjacent cells (Butterweck et al., 1994; Langlois et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature and is inferred from the connexin expression.

claim: A brief photoactivation of ArchT in actuator cells induced a ~ 4.3% ∆F/F0 increase in pHluorinCAAX fluorescence in neighboring receiver cells.
source: When ArchT and pHluorin were separately expressed in neighboring cells (i.e. in the trans configuration, see Materials and methods; Figure 1B1), a brief photoactivation of ArchT in the actuator cells (4 s,~0.5 mW, indicated by the yellow circle in Figure 1B2) faithfully induced a ~ 4.3% ∆F/F0 increase in pHluorinCAAX fluorescence in the neighboring receiver cells whereas non-adjacent pHluorinCAAX-expressing cells had no measurable change in fluorescence (Figures 1B2–B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B2–B3.

claim: Non-adjacent pHluorinCAAX-expressing cells had no measurable change in fluorescence upon photoactivation of ArchT in actuator cells.
source: When ArchT and pHluorin were separately expressed in neighboring cells (i.e. in the trans configuration, see Materials and methods; Figure 1B1), a brief photoactivation of ArchT in the actuator cells (4 s,~0.5 mW, indicated by the yellow circle in Figure 1B2) faithfully induced a ~ 4.3% ∆F/F0 increase in pHluorinCAAX fluorescence in the neighboring receiver cells whereas non-adjacent pHluorinCAAX-expressing cells had no measurable change in fluorescence (Figures 1B2–B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B2–B3 and serves as a spatial control.

claim: Application of carbenoxolone (CBX, 100 μM) significantly decreased the light-induced PARIS signal.
source: Application of carbenoxolone (CBX, 100 μM) which blocks gap junctions (Connors, 2012) significantly decreased the light-induced PARIS signal (Figure 1C), confirming that the signal measured in receiver cells is mediated by GJC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating pharmacological blockade of the PARIS signal.

claim: Carbenoxolone (CBX) blocks gap junctions.
source: Application of carbenoxolone (CBX, 100 μM) which blocks gap junctions (Connors, 2012) significantly decreased the light-induced PARIS signal (Figure 1C), confirming that the signal measured in receiver cells is mediated by GJC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature on CBX function.

claim: The signal measured in receiver cells is mediated by GJC.
source: Application of carbenoxolone (CBX, 100 μM) which blocks gap junctions (Connors, 2012) significantly decreased the light-induced PARIS signal (Figure 1C), confirming that the signal measured in receiver cells is mediated by GJC.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the CBX blockade experiment showing that the signal depends on gap junction function.

claim: Increasing the duration of the illumination pulse from 1 s to 20 s incrementally increased the PARIS response from ~2% to~20%.
source: Similar to autonomous signals, increasing the duration of the illumination pulse from 1 s to 20 s incrementally increased the PARIS response from ~2% to~20% (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–E demonstrating a dose-response relationship.

claim: A 4 s laser pulse was sufficient to induce a robust PARIS signal with SNR = 23 ± 8.
source: A 4 s laser pulse was sufficient to induce a robust PARIS signal (SNR = 23 ± 8, Figure 1F) with a half-rise time of ~10 s (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: A 4 s laser pulse induces a PARIS signal with a half-rise time of ~10 s.
source: A 4 s laser pulse was sufficient to induce a robust PARIS signal (SNR = 23 ± 8, Figure 1F) with a half-rise time of ~10 s (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A 20 s laser pulse induced an ~4.3-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio compared to 4 s.
source: On the other hand, a 20 s laser pulse induced an ~4.3-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio compared to 4 s with a half-rise time of ~21 s (Figure 1F,G); however, the half-decay time did not differ between a 4 s pulse and a 20 s pulse (t1/2 decay = 61 ± 5s and 67 ± 3 s respectively, Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: A 20 s laser pulse induces a PARIS signal with a half-rise time of ~21 s.
source: On the other hand, a 20 s laser pulse induced an ~4.3-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio compared to 4 s with a half-rise time of ~21 s (Figure 1F,G); however, the half-decay time did not differ between a 4 s pulse and a 20 s pulse (t1/2 decay = 61 ± 5s and 67 ± 3 s respectively, Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The half-decay time did not differ between a 4 s pulse and a 20 s pulse (t1/2 decay = 61 ± 5s and 67 ± 3 s respectively).
source: On the other hand, a 20 s laser pulse induced an ~4.3-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio compared to 4 s with a half-rise time of ~21 s (Figure 1F,G); however, the half-decay time did not differ between a 4 s pulse and a 20 s pulse (t1/2 decay = 61 ± 5s and 67 ± 3 s respectively, Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Spatially graded PARIS signals were observed in three receiver cells that are sequentially connected to the actuator cell.
source: We also observed the spatially graded PARIS signals in three receiver cells that are sequentially connected to the actuator cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The directly connected cell had the strongest PARIS response, and the thirdly connected cell had the weakest response.
source: Specifically, the directly connected cell had the strongest response, and the thirdly connected cell had the weakest response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: A 4 s laser pulse induces a transient increase of intracellular pH from 7.35 to 7.45 in actuator cells.
source: Based on a fit to the titration curve, we estimated that a 4 s and 20 s laser pulse induces a transient increase of intracellular pH from 7.35 to 7.45 and 7.80 respectively in actuator cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–F), which allowed us to repeatedly elicit a PARIS signal in specific cells as shown above.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH calibration experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: A 20 s laser pulse induces a transient increase of intracellular pH from 7.35 to 7.80 in actuator cells.
source: Based on a fit to the titration curve, we estimated that a 4 s and 20 s laser pulse induces a transient increase of intracellular pH from 7.35 to 7.45 and 7.80 respectively in actuator cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–F), which allowed us to repeatedly elicit a PARIS signal in specific cells as shown above.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH calibration experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Applying increasingly stronger light pulses to the actuator cell yielded time-locked currents in the receiver cell that were blocked by CBX.
source: Applying increasingly stronger light pulses to the actuator cell yielded time-locked currents in the receiver cell that were blocked by CBX (Figure 2B2,D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2B2,D2.

claim: Voltage steps on the actuator cell elicited non-rectifying and CBX sensitive currents in the receiver cell.
source: In the same cells, voltage steps on the actuator cell also elicited non-rectifying and CBX sensitive currents in the receiver cell (Figure 2C,D3).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C,D3.

claim: The CBX inhibition of GJC was independent from the approaches used to activate the actuator cell (by light or voltage) and from the signals measured in the receiver cell (pHluorinCAAX fluorescence or currents).
source: Quantification of the group data showed that the CBX inhibition of GJC was independent from the approaches used to activate the actuator cell (by light or voltage) and from the signals measured in the receiver cell (pHluorinCAAX fluorescence or currents) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The PARIS signal was stable for five sequential pulses at 2 min intervals.
source: The PARIS signal was stable for five sequential pulses at 2 min intervals, whereas the FRAP signal decayed considerably over the same time period in terms of both basal fluorescence and SNR (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G–I comparing PARIS and FRAP.

claim: The FRAP signal decayed considerably over five sequential measurements in terms of both basal fluorescence and SNR.
source: The PARIS signal was stable for five sequential pulses at 2 min intervals, whereas the FRAP signal decayed considerably over the same time period in terms of both basal fluorescence and SNR (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G–I comparing PARIS and FRAP.

claim: The PARIS signal had considerably faster kinetics than FRAP, with a half-rise time of ~21 s compared to ~197 s, respectively.
source: Moreover, the PARIS signal had considerably faster kinetics than FRAP, with a half-rise time of ~21 s compared to ~197 s, respectively (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Phosphorylation has been implicated in the modulation of GJC by affecting the trafficking, assembly/disassembly, degradation and gating of gap junctions.
source: Phosphorylation has been implicated in the modulation of GJC by affecting the trafficking, assembly/disassembly, degradation and gating of gap junctions (Laird, 2005; Nihei et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on gap junction regulation.

claim: Treating cells with TPA significantly inhibited the PARIS signal compared to the control group.
source: Compared with the control group, treating cells with TPA significantly inhibited the PARIS signal compared to the control group; in contrast, neither 8-Br-cAMP nor forskolin had obvious effect (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that activating PKC—but not protein kinase A—inhibits GJC, which is in general consistent with previous reports (Lampe, 1994; Sirnes et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Neither 8-Br-cAMP nor forskolin had obvious effect on the PARIS signal.
source: Compared with the control group, treating cells with TPA significantly inhibited the PARIS signal compared to the control group; in contrast, neither 8-Br-cAMP nor forskolin had obvious effect (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that activating PKC—but not protein kinase A—inhibits GJC, which is in general consistent with previous reports (Lampe, 1994; Sirnes et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Activating PKC—but not protein kinase A—inhibits GJC.
source: Compared with the control group, treating cells with TPA significantly inhibited the PARIS signal compared to the control group; in contrast, neither 8-Br-cAMP nor forskolin had obvious effect (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that activating PKC—but not protein kinase A—inhibits GJC, which is in general consistent with previous reports (Lampe, 1994; Sirnes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: Mutations in GJA1, the gene encoding Cx43, have been linked to inherited oculodentodigital dysplasia.
source: Mutations in GJA1, the gene encoding Cx43, have been linked to a number of diseases such as the inherited oculodentodigital dysplasia (Paznekas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on GJA1 mutations and disease.

claim: HeLa cells do not express measurable levels of endogenous Cxs.
source: We performed PARIS in HeLa cells, which do not express measurable levels of endogenous Cxs (Elfgang et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on HeLa cell connexin expression.

claim: No PARIS signal was elicited in receiver HeLa cells upon photoactivating the actuator cell.
source: As expected, no PARIS signal was elicited in receiver HeLa cells upon photoactivating the actuator cell; while in HeLa cells expressing GJA1, photoactivating the actuator cell elicited a robust fluorescence increase in the adjacent receiver cell (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D and serves as a negative control.

claim: In HeLa cells expressing GJA1, photoactivating the actuator cell elicited a robust fluorescence increase in the adjacent receiver cell.
source: As expected, no PARIS signal was elicited in receiver HeLa cells upon photoactivating the actuator cell; while in HeLa cells expressing GJA1, photoactivating the actuator cell elicited a robust fluorescence increase in the adjacent receiver cell (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Expressing a Cx43 protein with either the R202H or R76H mutation caused a significant reduction in the PARIS signal compared to cells expressing wild-type Cx43.
source: Interestingly, expressing a Cx43 protein with either the R202H or R76H mutation—which affects Cx43 trafficking and gap junction permeability (Shibayama et al., 2005)—caused a significant reduction in the PARIS signal compared to cells expressing wild-type Cx43 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The R202H and R76H mutations affect Cx43 trafficking and gap junction permeability.
source: Interestingly, expressing a Cx43 protein with either the R202H or R76H mutation—which affects Cx43 trafficking and gap junction permeability (Shibayama et al., 2005)—caused a significant reduction in the PARIS signal compared to cells expressing wild-type Cx43 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on these Cx43 mutations.

claim: Gap junctions formed by Cx40, Cx43, and Cx45 play an important role in cardiomyocytes by synchronizing their contractions.
source: Gap junctions formed by Cx40, Cx43, and Cx45 play an important role in CMs by synchronizing their contractions and defects in these connexins have been associated with cardiovascular diseases (Jongsma and Wilders, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on cardiac gap junctions.

claim: Defects in Cx40, Cx43, and Cx45 have been associated with cardiovascular diseases.
source: Gap junctions formed by Cx40, Cx43, and Cx45 play an important role in CMs by synchronizing their contractions and defects in these connexins have been associated with cardiovascular diseases (Jongsma and Wilders, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on cardiac gap junctions and disease.

claim: Stimulating actuator cardiomyocytes induced a robust fluorescence increase in receiver cardiomyocytes with half-rise and half-decay times of approximately 14 and 21 s respectively.
source: Using CMs cultured from neonatal rats (Figure 3E), we observed that stimulating actuator CMs induced a robust fluorescence increase in receiver CMs with half-rise and half-decay times of approximately 14 and 21 s respectively, and the responses were reversibly blocked by the gap junction blocker heptanol (Garcia-Dorado et al., 1997) (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: The PARIS responses in cardiomyocytes were reversibly blocked by the gap junction blocker heptanol.
source: Using CMs cultured from neonatal rats (Figure 3E), we observed that stimulating actuator CMs induced a robust fluorescence increase in receiver CMs with half-rise and half-decay times of approximately 14 and 21 s respectively, and the responses were reversibly blocked by the gap junction blocker heptanol (Garcia-Dorado et al., 1997) (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: Heptanol is a gap junction blocker.
source: Using CMs cultured from neonatal rats (Figure 3E), we observed that stimulating actuator CMs induced a robust fluorescence increase in receiver CMs with half-rise and half-decay times of approximately 14 and 21 s respectively, and the responses were reversibly blocked by the gap junction blocker heptanol (Garcia-Dorado et al., 1997) (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on heptanol function.

claim: Neither the rate of spontaneous Ca2+ transients in cardiomyocytes nor the rate of cellular beating was altered by the expression or stimulation of the actuator protein.
source: Neither the rate of spontaneous Ca2+ transients in CMs nor the rate of cellular beating was altered by the expression or stimulation of the actuator protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the notion that expressing and activating PARIS does not affect cellular functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expressing and activating PARIS does not affect cellular functions.
source: Neither the rate of spontaneous Ca2+ transients in CMs nor the rate of cellular beating was altered by the expression or stimulation of the actuator protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the notion that expressing and activating PARIS does not affect cellular functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing no effects on Ca2+ transients or beating rate.

claim: ArchT and pHluorin can produce cell-autonomous signals in an ex vivo Drosophila brain preparation.
source: Using the Drosophila olfactory system as a model system, we first confirmed that ArchT and pHluorin can produce cell-autonomous signals in an ex vivo preparation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ePN autonomous signal could be elicited repeatedly in the same sample for up to 2 hr, with no obvious loss of signal strength.
source: The ePN autonomous signal could be elicited repeatedly in the same sample for up to 2 hr, with no obvious loss of signal strength (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I), indicating that PARIS is stable in intact living tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: PARIS is stable in intact living tissue.
source: The ePN autonomous signal could be elicited repeatedly in the same sample for up to 2 hr, with no obvious loss of signal strength (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I), indicating that PARIS is stable in intact living tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the stability of the signal over 2 hours.

claim: Excitatory projection neurons (ePNs) and excitatory local neurons (eLNs) both have dendritic arborizations in the antennal lobe (AL).

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on Drosophila olfactory system anatomy.

claim: Stimulating a 20 μm diameter region in the AL elicited a rapid increase in pHluorinCAAX fluorescence in eLNs, with half-rise and half-decay times of approximately 12 s and 29 s, respectively.
source: Stimulating a 20 μm diameter region in the AL elicited a rapid increase in pHluorinCAAX fluorescence, with half-rise and half-decay times of approximately 12 s and 29 s, respectively (Figure 4B,C,F,G), consistent with previously reported electrophysiological data indicating that ePNs and eLNs are electrically coupled (Huang et al., 2010; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies and confirmed by PARIS data.

claim: When activated, none of inhibitory local neurons (iLNs), glial cells, or Keyon cells caused a measurable PARIS signal in ePN receiver cells.
source: In addition, we examined gap junction activity between ePNs and other cell types by pairing ePNs as the receiver cells with various actuator cells that have anatomical overlap with ePNs, including inhibitory local neurons (iLNs), glial cells, and Keyon cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, second-bottom rows). However, when activated, none of these three cell types caused a measurable PARIS signal in the receiver cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that ePNs may not form functional gap junction connections with iLNs, glial cells, or Keyon cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: ePNs may not form functional gap junction connections with iLNs, glial cells, or Keyon cells.

However, when activated, none of these three cell types caused a measurable PARIS signal in the receiver cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that ePNs may not form functional gap junction connections with iLNs, glial cells, or Keyon cells.

claim: Ventrally localized inhibitory projection neurons (iPNs) and ePNs form gap junctions participating in odor information processing.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on Drosophila olfactory system connectivity.

claim: Both ePNs and iPNs have dendrites in the AL and axons that project to the lateral horn (LH).

claim: Stimulating the AL—but not the LH—elicited a significant increase in pHluorinCAAX fluorescence in ePNs when iPNs were the actuator cells.

claim: iPNs and ePNs form functional gap junctions at the AL (i.e. via dendrite-dendrite contacts), but not at the LH (i.e. via axon-axon contacts).

claim: Lari showed the best membrane trafficking performance and 26-times the light-sensitivity of ArchT.
source: By measuring the cell-autonomous pHluorin fluorescence increase in response to green-yellow light, we found that six candidates exhibited larger ΔF/F0 than ArchT with a fungi rhodopsin that we named Lari showed the best membrane trafficking performance and 26-times the light-sensitivity of ArchT (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lari provides a more powerful actuator for in vivo application of PARIS in the future.

claim: PARIS can be readily adapted for use in both in vitro and ex vivo preparations, including cultured cell lines, primary cardiomyocytes, and transgenic flies.
source: Here, we describe the development of PARIS, a new all-optical approach for detecting GJC in specific cells. We show that PARIS can be readily adapted for use in both in vitro and ex vivo preparations, including cultured cell lines, primary cardiomyocytes, and transgenic flies.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 1-5.

claim: PARIS specifically reports functional gap junctions as validated using a variety of electrophysiological, pharmacological, and genetic approaches.

evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the validation experiments shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: PARIS is the first completely genetically encoded method for probing electrical synapses.
source: By focusing on defined sets of neurons in the Drosophila olfactory system, we show that as the first completely genetically encoded method, PARIS can be applied to repeatedly probe electrical synapses in distinct, genetically tractable neurons with high temporal resolution (on the order of ~10 s) and high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of PARIS compared to existing methods.

claim: Light activation of BeCylOp generated limited cGMP that could not induce FlincG3 response.
source: For the cGMP based pair, we have also performed the cis experiments in the presence of PDE inhibitor IBMX that prevented the cGMP hydrolyzation and still observed no signal; meanwhile FlincG did response to exogenous application of cGMP (data not shown). Thus, one possible explanation for the absence of the autonomous signal is that light activation of BeCylOp generated limited cGMP that could not induce FlincG3 (EC50 = 0.89 μM) (Bhargava et al., 2013) response.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the negative result with the cGMP-based pair, supported by additional experiments and a citation.

claim: The photoactivation induced Ca2+ influx in the CsChrimson expressing HEK293T cells was still under the detection limit of GCaMP6s.
source: For the pair with CsChrimson, a non-selective cation channel allows not only Ca2+ but also other cations to pass the channel (Klapoetke et al., 2014), we deduce the photoactivation induced Ca2+ influx in the CsChrimson expressing HEK293T cells was still under the detection limit of GCaMP6s.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the negative result with the Ca2+-based pair, based on the properties of CsChrimson.

claim: CsChrimson/GCaMP6s could function in cis to generate cell autonomous signals in cultured hippocampus neurons that endogenously express voltage-gated Ca2+ channel to allow further Ca2+ influx.
source: Indeed, we found CsChrimson/GCaMP6s could function in cis to generate cell autonomous signals in cultured hippocampus neurons that endogenously express voltage-gated Ca2+ channel to allow further Ca2+ influx (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is mentioned but the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: PARIS relies solely on light and therefore is virtually non-invasive compared with existing methods including paired-recording, dye microinjection and scrape loading.
source: First, PARIS relies solely on light and therefore is virtually non-invasive compared with existing methods including paired-recording (Bennett et al., 1963; Furshpan and Potter, 1959), dye microinjection (Stewart, 1978) and scrape loading (el-Fouly et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a comparison of PARIS to existing methods, supported by citations.

claim: The activation of the actuator can be specific to subcellular resolution, allowing PARIS to provide spatial information of the functional gap junctions.
source: In addition, given that the activation of the actuator can be specific to subcellular resolution, PARIS can provide spatial information of the functional gap junctions, as shown by our ability to functionally map gap junctions formed at dendrite-dendrite contacts in AL but not at axon-axon contacts in LH between ePNs and iPNs in the Drosophila olfactory system (Figure 5), while such resolution cannot be easily achieved by any of the previously existed method.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data in Figure 5 showing subcellular resolution.

claim: PARIS is fully reversible and does not require the delivery of exogenous dyes.
source: With respect to those relatively non-invasive methods which rely on the diffusion of small fluorescent dyes across gap junctions such as FRAP (Wade et al., 1986) and LAMP (Dakin et al., 2005), a significant advantage of PARIS is that it is fully reversible and does not require the delivery of exogenous dyes.
evidence: This is a comparison of PARIS to dye-based methods, highlighting its advantages.

source: PARIS may serve as a robust tool for screening existing and newly developed gap junction blockers and/or modulators, including clinically relevant compounds such as inhibitors of PKC signaling.

evidence: This is a statement about potential delivery methods for PARIS components.

claim: Intracellular pH is believed to be tightly regulated for optimal biochemical reactions in most animal cells.
source: In most animal cells, intracellular pH is believed to be tightly regulated for optimal biochemical reactions; thus, even a small change in intracellular pH is rapidly restored to a set point by buffers and proton exchangers/transporters located on the membrane of cells or intracellular organelles (Hoffmann and Simonsen, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pH homeostasis, supported by a citation.

claim: The uncoupling effect of acidic intracellular pH on GJC has long been described across different Cx-consisted gap junctions in vertebrates and different innexin-consisted gap junctions in invertebrates.
source: The uncoupling effect of acidic intracellular pH on GJC has long been described across different Cx-consisted gap junctions in vertebrates (Peracchia, 2004; Turin and Warner, 1977) and different innexin-consisted gap junctions in invertebrates (Giaume et al., 1980; Obaid et al., 1983; Stergiopoulos et al., 1999), while alkalization was reported to increase the junctional conductance and the total number of opened channels in gap junction plagues (Palacios-Prado et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on pH effects on gap junctions.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on Cx43 pH sensitivity.

claim: A control experiment in the cis configuration is recommended in different customized preparations and context to ensure the function of the actuators and help to optimize the expression level of actuators/receivers as well as the photostimulation parameters accordingly.
source: Lastly, to protect against false negatives of PARIS, a control experiment in the cis configuration is recommended in different customized preparations and context to ensure the function of the actuators and help to optimize the expression level of actuators/receivers as well as the photostimulation parameters accordingly; Meanwhile, PARIS signals alone from cells connected by potential unknown gap junctions should not be interpreted as definitive without confirmation from pharmacology, genetic interventions or a complementary method.
